demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette:
Leilani Faleolo is a 61-year-old Samoan-American woman who has worked as a security guard at a large commercial warehouse on the outskirts of Phoenix for the past eleven years. She came to the clinic on a referral from her employee assistance programme, presenting with a PCL-5 score of 76 and a demeanour that her intake worker described as carefully composed - the kind of stillness that suggests long practice at holding something very still.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Leilani was conducting a routine perimeter check during a night shift. The warehouse loading dock was poorly lit in one section where a maintenance request had gone unaddressed for weeks. She was driving the facility's electric patrol cart along a route she had driven hundreds of times before. A young seasonal worker, a man in his mid-twenties named Darius, had crouched behind a pallet stack to retrieve a dropped item and was invisible to her in the darkness and her peripheral blind spot. She did not see him. The cart struck him at low speed, but the angle and the concrete surface meant the impact fractured his pelvis and caused internal injuries that required emergency surgery and a hospitalisation of several weeks. Leilani was the one who called for help, who stayed with him on the ground, who heard the specific wet sound he made when she found him. Darius survived and has since returned to work elsewhere, but Leilani has never spoken to him again.

In the weeks following the incident, Leilani found herself returning obsessively to the sequence of events - the exact moment she turned the wheel, whether she had been looking straight ahead or slightly to the left, whether she had been moving faster than usual. She could not stop going over the details, looking for the precise point at which she had done something wrong, as though if she could only locate it clearly enough she could understand how a person like her - careful, experienced, responsible - had come to hurt someone. She also found herself asking a broader, more bewildering question: why this had happened to her at all, after so many years of doing her job without incident. Neither line of inquiry has ever resolved.

What makes Leilani's experience particularly disorienting is the texture of the memory itself. There are portions of the event she cannot recover no matter how deliberately she tries - specifically, the moments just before impact, which remain entirely absent, a gap she finds both distressing and, she has admitted, faintly shameful, as though her own mind is withholding evidence. At other times she can recount the sequence of events in what sounds like precise detail, but in those moments the account feels oddly evacuated - she speaks in a flat, measured tone, as though reading from a report about someone else entirely. She has described the memory as feeling like it belongs to a different woman, one she watches from a distance without recognition. This quality frightens her, because she had come to believe that a person who genuinely felt remorse would be unable to detach from what they had done. The numbness, when it comes, reads to her as evidence of a moral failure she cannot name.

Over the following months, Leilani continued to show up for her shifts - she could not afford not to - but her relationship to the work changed in ways that became visible to her supervisor. She began requesting indoor posts and offered various logistical justifications for avoiding the loading dock area. When those requests were no longer accommodatable, she began calling in sick on nights when she was rostered to that section. She has not driven the patrol cart since the incident, telling her supervisor that a knee problem makes it uncomfortable. Her supervisor has grown visibly impatient, and Leilani is now at risk of a formal performance review.

What finally brought her in was a conversation with her younger sister, who told her plainly that she had become unreachable - that she cancelled plans, deflected questions, and seemed to be disappearing into herself. Leilani sat with that for two weeks before making the appointment. What she is most afraid of, she said in her first session, is that there is no version of this story in which she is not simply someone who hurt a person and cannot find a way to live with that. What she is hoping for, more quietly, is that someone might help her understand what actually happened - and why she cannot seem to remember it clearly enough to know for certain.
